title: GL-Cache: Group-level learning for efficient and high-performance caching
one_line: A learned cache-eviction policy that clusters objects into write-time groups (log-structured segments), learns each group's utility with an XGBoost model over 6-7 group-level features, and evicts whole low-utility groups via merge-based eviction, amortizing learning overhead to under 1 byte and one inference per thousands of objects.

repo.evidence: Paper's 'Availability' section (paper.txt p. 14): 'We open-source our implementation at https://github.com/Thesys-lab/fast23-glcache' - which is the cloned repo. Repo is under the authors' lab org (Thesys-lab, CMU), README cites the FAST'23 paper and contains both artifacts described in paper 4.1: micro-implementation/ (libCacheSim snapshot, C) and prototype/ (Pelikan Segcache snapshot, Rust). The GLCache algorithm itself is fully present at micro-implementation/libCacheSim/cache/eviction/GLCache/ (11 source files implementing grouping, utility, training, inference, merge eviction, ghost entries).
repo.badge_evidence: none found - sysartifacts.github.io/fast states FAST introduced artifact evaluation in 2024, so a FAST'23 paper cannot carry badges; the repo makes no badge claim.

H1_open_repo.evidence: Official per paper Availability section (p. 14). Contains the real system, not a placeholder: micro-implementation/libCacheSim/cache/eviction/GLCache/{GLCache.c,GLCacheInternal.h,dataPrep.c,train.c,inference.c,segSel.c,segment.c,eviction.c,init.c,obj.h,const.h} implement every design component of paper 3.3-3.6, and prototype/src/l2cache/ holds the Rust prototype. Apache-2.0 (README.md:42-55, micro-implementation/LICENSE).

H2_no_root.evidence: Pure user-space trace-driven simulation; no kernel module, eBPF, perf counter, KVM, or /proc/sys use anywhere in the eviction code or the cachesim harness. The sudo grep hits are confined to dependency-install docs (micro-implementation/scripts/setup.sh:5,27,38,50; .travis.yml:51) and a fully commented-out CI file (.github/workflows/build.yml:22,56); both cmake/Modules/FindGLib.cmake:30-34 and FindZSTD.cmake:93-94 resolve via pkg-config, so a conda-forge env or a $HOME-prefix source build satisfies them. USE_HUGEPAGE (default ON, CMakeLists.txt:46) is only madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) at dataStructure/hashtable/chainedHashtable.c:96-99 and chainedHashTableV2.c:94-96 - unprivileged - and can be disabled with -DUSE_HUGEPAGE=OFF. The 'pmem' flag is a doc comment at prototype/src/l2cache/src/datapool/file.rs:6, not a requirement.

H3_hardware_fit.evidence: Single-node, CPU-only, no GPU anywhere. Paper 4.1 ran the micro-implementation on a CloudLab m510 (Xeon D-1548, 64 GB) - strictly weaker than this machine's 16 cores / 125 GB. The micro-implementation stores only eviction metadata, not object values (micro-implementation/README.md:19; paper 4.1), so a simulated 16 GB cache costs far less than 16 GB RAM. Traces are ~20 GB compressed for CloudPhysics+MSR and 23 GB for Wikimedia, inside the ~250 GB free. Sweeps across traces parallelize over 16 cores via cachesim --num-thread (bin/cachesim/cli.c:58).

H4_obtainable_deps_data.evidence: Deps are glib-2.0, zstd, tcmalloc (optional), XGBoost, cmake>=3.12, gcc (CMakeLists.txt:140-185) - all conda-forge / user-space installable and discovered via pkg-config. Data: all 118 traces are public at https://ftp.pdl.cmu.edu/pub/datasets/twemcacheWorkload/fast23_glcache/ (listing verified: cloudphysics/ has 106 w*.oracleGeneral.bin.zst files 11 MB-781 MB, msr/ has 14 files 14 MB-665 MB, wiki_2016u.oracleGeneral.zst is 23 GB), in the exact binary format the simulator reads (README.md:30-38). No proprietary traces, no model weights, no gated downloads. A 220 KB smoke trace ships in-repo at micro-implementation/data/trace.oracleGeneral.bin.

reproduce.target: Fig. 7(a)+7(c) (hit-ratio increase over FIFO, box plots over CloudPhysics and MSR traces at the small cache size) together with Fig. 8(a)+8(c) (throughput relative to FIFO). These support the paper's core claim that group-level learning attains learned-cache hit ratios at near-FIFO throughput: GL-Cache-E at or above LHD at the median while keeping >=50% of FIFO throughput, and GL-Cache-T near 0.8x FIFO throughput.
reproduce.scale_down: Drop the LRB bar (LRB is not in this repo - grep for LRB/lrb hits only README.md - and would need a separate build of the LRB authors' C++/LightGBM project); reproduce FIFO/LRU/Cacheus/LHD/GL-Cache-E/GL-Cache-T, all present in bin/cachesim/cli.c:271-335. Use a size-stratified sample of ~20-30 of the 103 CloudPhysics traces plus all 14 MSR traces instead of all 103. Cache sizes 1 GB and 16 GB for CloudPhysics (paper 4.1); 'auto' sizing for MSR. Warmup --warmup-sec=259200 (3 days), cross-checked at 86400 (Fig. 14). Run miss-ratio sweeps multi-threaded but throughput sweeps with --num-thread=1, since the multi-size path defaults to 16 threads (cli.c:58, main.c:31-33) and would corrupt MQPS.
reproduce.effort: ~5 person-days (2 build/deps, 1 trace download, 2 harness+plotting) + ~150-300 CPU-core-hours of simulation; 0 GPU-hours. Roughly 1-2 days wall clock for the sweep on 16 cores.
reproduce.rationale: Not H: there is no evaluation script, no plotting code, no trace-download script and no figure-to-command mapping anywhere in the repo (the only scripts are scripts/setup.sh and scripts/dataGen.py); the install docs assume root; the CI file has every hosted-runner job commented out so there is no public green build; CMakeLists.txt:120-122 clobbers CFLAGS and drops -std=gnu99 while GNU extensions (strsep in GLCache.c:50, strcasestr in cli.c:268) are used, so build fixes are likely; XGBoost >=2.x may have moved the C API in train.c/inference.c; and the LRB baseline behind half the headline claim is absent. Not L: the driver binary emits exactly the two plotted metrics natively (object miss ratio + MQPS at bin/cachesim/sim.c:68-81, object + byte miss ratio at bin/cachesim/main.c:55-67), every non-LRB baseline is in-tree, both GL-Cache operating points are specified verbatim in paper 4.1 and map onto CLI parameters parsed at GLCache.c:55-99, all traces are public in the simulator's native format, and the workload is CPU-only and well within this machine.

addons.name: Byte-aware group utility
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that replacing GL-Cache's size-penalizing group utility U = sum 1/(T*s) (and its matching 1/(size*age) object-retention score) with a size-neutral / byte-oriented variant improves byte miss ratio by >=10% under CloudPhysics, MSR and Wikimedia trace replay, at a bounded object-miss-ratio cost and without losing GL-Cache's throughput advantage over LHD and LRB.
addons.mechanism: Introduce an exponent alpha on the object-size term and expose it as a CLI eviction parameter, applied consistently at the three places the size term appears: the online training label (dataPrep.c:254, train_utility += 1e6/age/obj_size -> .../pow(obj_size, alpha)); the object retention score OBJ_SCORE_AGE_BYTE (obj.h:63-64, 1e8/size/age); and the prediction normalization by segment bytes (inference.c:107-110, pred*1e6/n_byte). Register 'utility-alpha' in the parameter parser (GLCache.c:55-99) and defaults (GLCache.c:25-43). Add byte miss ratio to the single-size output path (bin/cachesim/sim.c:68-81) - the multi-size path already computes it at main.c:59-64, so this is ~5 lines. Sweep alpha in {0, 0.5, 1} and plot the object-MR / byte-MR / throughput Pareto surface, extending the paper's Fig. 13.
addons.motivating_evidence: 3L-Cache (FAST'25) reports that among learning-based policies 'GL-Cache has the lowest object miss ratio, but its byte miss ratio is the worst, even higher than LRU'. The GL-Cache paper never reports byte miss ratio anywhere: 4.1 says it deliberately changed 'the LRB optimization target from byte miss ratio to object miss ratio', and Eq. 1-2 (3.4) bakes an explicit 1/s_o into the utility so that groups of large objects are systematically ranked for eviction. The code confirms the bias is hard-wired in three independent places (dataPrep.c:254, obj.h:63, inference.c:107). This is a published, externally identified weakness with an untested one-parameter fix.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Under ~200 LOC across five files, all localized; no new evaluation harness is needed because the existing cachesim multi-size path already computes and prints byte miss ratio (bin/cachesim/main.c:59-64); the sweep is the same one used for the reproduction, so it costs no extra infrastructure and fits this machine's CPU budget.
addons.research_value_rationale: A FAST'25 paper names this exact failure of GL-Cache and works around it by building a different, object-level learner that costs 3-6x LRU. Showing that GL-Cache's own utility can be re-weighted to reach competitive byte miss ratio at GL-Cache's throughput would establish a genuinely new point on the efficiency/throughput Pareto frontier. Showing it cannot would establish that high byte miss ratio is intrinsic to merge-based group eviction - you cannot selectively retain large objects when you evict whole groups - which is an equally informative negative result. Either outcome answers a question a FAST reviewer would ask.

scoop_check.details: Queries: '"GL-Cache" cache eviction comparison S3-FIFO SIEVE learned cache 2024'; '3L-Cache FAST 2025 Zhou Wenbin ... GL-Cache byte miss ratio'; '"group-level learning" cache eviction improve grouping heuristic multi-feature buckets segment utility 2025 2026'. Closest work: 3L-Cache, FAST'25 (https://www.usenix.org/conference/fast25/presentation/zhou-wenbin) identifies GL-Cache's byte-miss-ratio weakness and achieves the best byte and object miss ratios, but does so with a different object-level learned design plus bidirectional sampling; it does not modify GL-Cache's group utility function. No work found that re-weights GL-Cache's utility.

addons.name: Multi-key grouping (activate the dead multi-bucket path)
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that grouping objects by (write time x object-size class) rather than write time alone improves object miss ratio under traces with heterogeneous object sizes (Wikimedia CDN, MSR and CloudPhysics at small cache sizes), because groups become more homogeneous in utility and the learned model no longer has to average over widely differing object sizes.
addons.mechanism: const.h:3 hard-codes #define MAX_N_BUCKET 1, but the entire multi-bucket machinery already exists and loops over MAX_N_BUCKET: per-bucket segment chains and ranked chains (segSel.c:94, segSel.c:155-172), bucket round-robin selection (segSel.c:202-241), inference (inference.c:50, inference.c:101), training snapshots (dataPrep.c:217), and bucket init (init.c:87-93). Raise MAX_N_BUCKET to K; replace the hard-coded bucket choice at insertion (GLCache.c:312, bucket = &params->buckets[0]) with an assignment from floor(log2(req->obj_size)); make cross-bucket utility ranking fair in rank_segs (segSel.c:84-173); optionally add the bucket key as a model feature (dataPrep.c:105-110 plus n_feature at init.c:58). Measure the interaction with the existing 'evicting and cannot merge' fragmentation fallback (GLCache.c:352-368), which becomes far more likely with K buckets.
addons.motivating_evidence: Paper 3.3 explicitly leaves this unexplored: 'Depending on workload types, such features include time, tenant id, content type, object size, etc. In this work, we focus on grouping based on write time, which is available in all systems and hence more generalizable.' Fig. 2a shows the advantage of write-time grouping (lower coefficient of variation of mean reuse time vs random grouping) shrinks toward random grouping as group size increases - i.e. the grouping key is the weak link precisely at the large S_group where GL-Cache-T operates. Fig. 9c shows object size is the single most important feature at the 1 GB cache size, suggesting size is a natural clustering key. And the code shows the multi-bucket path is dead code (const.h:3 MAX_N_BUCKET 1), so the authors wrote but never evaluated the machinery this add-on turns on.
addons.feasibility_rationale: The bucket loops, per-bucket chains and ranked-chain plumbing already exist; the change is bucket assignment at insertion plus repairing whatever breaks in cross-bucket ranking and merging - roughly 300-600 LOC in one module. Evaluated with the same cachesim harness and traces used for the reproduction, on this machine.
addons.research_value_rationale: A natural extension the paper itself flags rather than a surprising one; a reviewer would expect grouping by size to help somewhat. The genuinely interesting sub-questions - does finer grouping beat the write-time locality that motivated the log-structured design, and how badly does bucketing fragment the segment pool and trigger the no-merge fallback - are real but of moderate interest, and the risk that the dead path is simply buggy makes the payoff uncertain.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'learned cache eviction grouping objects by size class or TTL bucket instead of write time group-level learning segment'; '"group-level learning" cache eviction improve grouping heuristic multi-feature buckets segment utility 2025 2026'; 'GL-Cache group-level learning follow-up work citing improve grouping segment cache eviction 2024 2025'. Nothing found that changes GL-Cache's grouping key or evaluates multi-key group formation. The nearest follow-ups (3L-Cache FAST'25, SL-Cache DASFAA'26, Cold-RL arXiv 2508.12485, LAH arXiv 2608.27975) are all object-level or cache-level learners that do not group objects at all.

addons.name: Learned object retention inside the merge
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that replacing the fixed 1/(size*age) object-retention score used during merge-based eviction with a group-conditioned learned object score (reusing the per-object frequency the cache already tracks) improves hit ratio by closing >=30% of the gap between GL-Cache and the oracle-assisted group eviction of Fig. 5, under CloudPhysics and MSR replay, at no more than 2x GL-Cache's eviction cost.
addons.mechanism: obj.h:47-88 already enumerates six object score types (FREQ, FREQ_BYTE, FREQ_AGE, FREQ_AGE_BYTE, AGE_BYTE, ORACLE) but GLCache.c:135-137 hard-wires OBJ_SCORE_AGE_BYTE for the learned mode with no CLI knob. Step 1 (baseline): expose obj-score-type as a parameter in the parser (GLCache.c:55-99) and quantify what the existing alternatives buy. Step 2 (contribution): add a score type whose weights over (freq, age, size) are fit online, using the ghost-entry reuse signal the cache already accumulates (dataPrep.c:244-257) as the label - either a tiny per-cache linear model or weights derived from the group model's predicted utility. Plumb through find_cutoff (segment.c:145-172) and GLCache_merge_segs (eviction.c:87-103). Use the in-tree oracle variants type=twoOracle / type=itemOracle (GLCacheInternal.h:8-13) to get the Fig. 5 upper bound for free.
addons.motivating_evidence: Paper 3.6 is candid that the object-retention metric is an unjustified heuristic: 'object selection uses a simple metric based on object age and size: 1/(size*age) where age is the time since the last access. We choose to use this metric because recency and size are the two most common metrics used in other eviction algorithms.' Fig. 5 (4.2) shows oracle-assisted group eviction matches size-aware Belady, so group granularity is not the bottleneck and the remaining gap in the deployed system sits in the utility prediction plus this retention heuristic. Critically, 4.5 / Fig. 9a shows frequency is the joint-highest-importance feature at the group level (median importance ~0.3), yet frequency is entirely absent from the object score that decides which individual objects survive a merge (obj.h:63, OBJ_SCORE_AGE_BYTE).
addons.feasibility_rationale: The score-type enum, the per-merge score array, the cutoff machinery (segment.c:145-172) and the ghost-entry label pipeline (dataPrep.c:244-257) all already exist; the minimal version is a new branch in cal_obj_score plus a weight-update hook, and the oracle upper bounds are already selectable via -e type=twoOracle. Comfortably within 10 weeks for 2-4 students on this machine.
addons.research_value_rationale: Well-motivated by the paper's own admission and measurable against a clean oracle upper bound (Fig. 5). But the direction - 'apply learning to the second level too' - is what a reviewer would expect next, and the achievable gain is explicitly bounded by Fig. 5, so the result is unlikely to surprise even if it works.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'segment merge eviction retain objects learned score Segcache GL-Cache improve object retention policy research'; '"SL-Cache" selective learning cache eviction priority retention hot objects GL-Cache group'. Closest work: SL-Cache, DASFAA 2026 (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-92-0363-5_36) uses an adaptive hotness-aware sampling strategy so that hot objects are retained and non-hot candidates are selected for prediction or eviction - conceptually similar retention logic, but at the object-sampling level of an object-level learner, not inside a group merge, and it does not modify GL-Cache.

addons.name: Adaptive learning cadence (self-tuning retrain and rank intervals)
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that a closed-loop controller that sets retrain_intvl and rank_intvl from signals GL-Cache already computes (validation RMSE drift across retrainings, observed interval miss-ratio degradation) improves hit ratio by recovering most of the 'up to 10%' the paper attributes to per-workload retraining-interval tuning, under the full CloudPhysics and MSR trace set and without per-workload tuning, at no more than 10% throughput cost.
addons.mechanism: The retrain trigger is a fixed wall-clock comparison against retrain_intvl = 86400 (GLCache.c:288-303; default set at GLCache.c:30). The training loop already parses per-round train/valid RMSE and early-stops on stability (train.c:55-76), but last_valid_loss is a local and is discarded. Persist it into learner_t (GLCacheInternal.h:43-72) and add a controller: lengthen the interval when the new model's validation loss is close to the previous one and the cache's tracked miss ratio (cacheState.h, GLCacheInternal.h:74-86) is stable; shorten it when either jumps. Apply the same idea to the re-ranking cadence at segSel.c:343 (ranked_seg_pos >= n_ranked_segs * rank_intvl), trading inference cost against staleness. Evaluate against an offline per-trace sweep of fixed retrain-intvl values, which gives the per-workload-tuned upper bound the controller must approach, and check that the controller does not reintroduce the metastable-failure risk the paper cites as its reason for using wall-clock time.
addons.motivating_evidence: Paper 4.6 states the opportunity and its size verbatim: 'the best retraining interval depends on the workload - some workloads show higher hit ratios with half-day retraining, and some others benefit from two-day retraining. While fine-tuning retraining intervals can improve the hit ratio by up to 10%, one-day retraining achieves a good performance across workloads.' The code confirms the interval is a fixed constant (GLCache.c:30, retrain_intvl = 86400) and that the validation-loss signal needed to drive a controller is already computed but thrown away (train.c:68-76). Paper 3.5 also argues wall-clock retraining avoids metastable failure under load spikes, which is a real constraint any controller must respect rather than a free lunch.
addons.feasibility_rationale: All required signals are already computed inside the cache; the change is confined to the trigger logic plus one persisted struct field, well under 500 LOC. Evaluation is the base sweep plus a fixed-interval oracle sweep, roughly 3x the reproduction compute - still affordable on 16 cores with no GPU.
addons.research_value_rationale: The paper itself identifies the gap and bounds it at 10%, so the ceiling is known and modest, and dynamic training-frequency adjustment has already been demonstrated for object-level learned caches. It remains worth doing because nobody has shown whether the coarser group-level signal is strong enough to drive such a controller, and because the metastable-failure constraint makes the safe design non-obvious - but a reviewer would call the direction expected.

scoop_check.details: Queries: '3L-Cache FAST 2025 Zhou Wenbin low overhead precise learning cache eviction'; '"GL-Cache" cache eviction comparison S3-FIFO SIEVE learned cache 2024'. Closest work: 3L-Cache, FAST'25 (https://www.usenix.org/conference/fast25/presentation/zhou-wenbin) introduces 'an efficient training data collection scheme that filters out unnecessary historical cache requests and dynamically adjusts the training frequency' plus 'a parameter auto-tuning method to enhance adaptability across traces' - the same idea, but applied to an object-level learner, not to GL-Cache's group-level model or its segment-ranking cadence.

risks: The LRB baseline is absent from the repo (grep for LRB/lrb across repo/ hits only README.md), so the headline claims '228x higher throughput' and '+7% hit ratio vs LRB' (Abstract, 4.4, Table 4) cannot be reproduced without separately building the LRB authors' C++/LightGBM project and its trace pipeline. TinyLFU and Cachelib (Fig. 6) are likewise missing.

Feature-count discrepancy between paper and code: 3.5 and Fig. 9a claim seven features including write rate, but the micro-implementation compiles six (const.h:19 N_FEATURE_NORMAL 6, N_FEATURE_TIME_WINDOW 0; dataPrep.c:105-110 writes age, mean obj size, n_hit, n_active, req_rate, miss_ratio). write_rate is tracked on the segment (GLCacheInternal.h:116, GLCache.c:319-321) and averaged on merge (eviction.c:79-80) but never enters the model. Fig. 9 cannot be reproduced exactly.

Build friction: CMakeLists.txt:120-122 overwrites CFLAGS on Linux and drops -std=gnu99 while GNU extensions are used (strsep at GLCache.c:50-51, strcasestr at cli.c:268), so -D_GNU_SOURCE fixes are likely with gcc 12. find_package(xgboost REQUIRED) (CMakeLists.txt:181) needs XGBoost's CMake config package, which conda-forge may not ship - falling back to a source build into $HOME/local. XGBoost >=2.x may have moved the C API used in train.c/inference.c; pin ~1.7 (paper-era) first. No public CI signal: every hosted-runner job in .github/workflows/build.yml is commented out, leaving only a self-hosted job.

The Rust prototype is the risky half: prototype/Cargo.toml:26 and prototype/src/l2cache/Cargo.toml:45-60 pull three git dependencies (twitter/rustcommon, 1a1a11a/rustcommon, 1a1a11a/rust-xgboost rev 360af10). Cargo.lock pins revisions but the upstream repos must still resolve, and the old rust-xgboost bindings need bindgen/clang (not installed; conda-installable). If any fails, Fig. 6 and Fig. 13(a) are out of reach - treat the micro-implementation as the deliverable.

Throughput measurement is easy to get wrong: only the single-size path reports MQPS (bin/cachesim/sim.c:68-75) while the multi-size path defaults to 16 threads (cli.c:58, main.c:31-33). Throughput runs must be single-threaded, and this is a shared machine per env.md, so numbers will be noisier than the paper's dedicated CloudLab nodes - report medians over repeats.

Non-determinism: bin/cachesim/sim.c:16-17 seeds the RNG from time(NULL) and next_rand() drives the fallback segment-selection paths (segSel.c:183, segSel.c:306), so runs are not bit-reproducible. Pin the seed before any A/B comparison of an add-on.

Frozen artifact: last commit 2023-05-12, 0 open issues, no releases, no top-level license file in the driver's file scan (README.md:42-55 states Apache-2.0 and micro-implementation/LICENSE exists). Author support is unlikely. The maintained upstream github.com/1a1a11a/libCacheSim still ships GLCache and has scripts/install_dependency.sh, making it a lower-risk build target, but it has diverged from this FAST'23 snapshot - choosing which tree to modify is an early decision with real consequences for comparability.

Storage and download: ~20 GB (CloudPhysics + MSR) plus 23 GB compressed Wikimedia over HTTP from a university FTP mirror; the Rust prototype needs traces decompressed (prototype/README.md:20), putting Wikimedia at roughly 67 GB uncompressed. It fits in ~250 GB free but with less slack than it first appears.

Unsettled by reading: whether the multi-bucket code path used by add-on A2 is correct. It has never been exercised with MAX_N_BUCKET > 1, and DEBUG_ASSERTs at segSel.c:392-396 and eviction.c:60-61 assume all merged segments share a bucket. 'The dead path is broken' is a plausible early finding; budget debugging time.

Scoop pressure in this area is high and recent: 3L-Cache (FAST'25) and the LAH/S4-FIFO preprint (arXiv:2608.27975, Aug 2026) both benchmark against GL-Cache, and LAH already claims the offline-pretrained, zero-shot-transferable model idea. Any add-on must be checked against those two before the proposal is written.
